Quell: Reflect is 88 levels that fit perfectly into the rest of the series; the levels are generally well designed, pretty, and range from slightly to very complex. I found the levels on average to be much more difficult than the original Quell, but the game is very generous with hint coins if you are going for perfects, and it still ended with me having more than enough hint coins at the end. The sound design is still fantastic on both the sound effects and the music sides. My only notable complaint was that the difficulty felt very inconsistent. Some levels easily took me twenty or more minutes to solve, but it would be proceeded and followed by levels that took less than a minute each.

Quell: Reflect took me about 6 hours to finish and I 100% it on my first playthrough.

This game is an absolute joy for puzzle lovers. Quell Reflect combines simple mechanics with intricate level design that keeps you thinking. The visuals are stunning in a minimalist way, and the music is incredibly soothing. I love how the game slowly builds in difficulty, making each new puzzle rewarding without feeling overwhelming. [h1]●ゲームの説明[/h1]

　一方向に壁や動かない物体が無い限り、延々と滑り続ける水滴を操作してアイテムを集めるパズルゲーム

　ただクリアするのではなく、ステージ毎に指定された移動回数以内でクリアする事と、ステージ内に隠された宝石を見つけ出すという、チャレンジ要素と探索要素がある。
　指定数はほぼ最善手で、割とシビアな設定だ。

　プレイ時間は謎解き出来る能力によって個人差があるだろうが、十時間以内、もしくは前後にクリアできる程度。
　指定数以内を意識せず、ただクリアを目指すのであれば、数時間でクリア出来るかもしれない。

　音楽はクラシックのみ。他のゲーム（パズル等）で良く聞くタイプのBGM。

　ゲーム内で貰えるコインを使用して、ステージのヒント（指定数でクリアできる水滴の動きのガイド、宝石の位置）を見ることが出来る。

　操作説明はゲーム内の“オプション”→“コントロール”→“見る”から見れる。一応、下に有用なショートカットキーを記述する。

▼Rキー：やり直し
▼Uキー：一つ前に戻る
▼Hキー：次のステージへ

　デフォルトだと英語なので、オプションで日本語にしたほうが良いかもしれない。



[h1]●良い点[/h1]

[b]・頭を使う[/b]
　指定数以内を目指す場合は、かなり頭を使う。何手も先を予想する。なので思考力を必要としているゲームをしたいのであれば、お薦めできる。
　詰将棋みたいな思考の仕方をするので、詰将棋が好きならこれも良いかもしれない。


[b]・難しいという人の為のヒント機能[/b]
　もう分からん。という風になってもクリアだけはさせてくれる。実績等にも影響しないはずなので、安心して使用できる。



[h1]●微妙な点[/h1]

[b]・ゲーム終了時の挙動[/b]
　通常はタイトル画面で右上の×印か、Escキーを押して終了できる。
　しかし、アプリ画面の右上にある×印。ではなく、その更に右上のウィンドウ画面に付いている閉じるボタンで終了させると、正しく終了されない事が多い。（タスクバーからは消えるが、プロセスは終了していない）

　そういう場合はSteamアプリで終了ボタンを押すか、タスクマネージャーを使うしかない。
　知らずに放置していると負荷が無駄に生じるかもしれない。


[b]・UIの配置が悪い[/b]
　全く使いにくいという訳ではないが、画面遷移後のボタンの位置がウロウロするので、若干だが操作のしにくさを感じる。



[h1]●悪い点[/h1]

[b]・ステージセレクト[/b]
　ステージセレクト時の挙動が少し悪い。

　ロード時間と画面遷移に五秒近く経過する。
　またステージ攻略時にステージセレクトしたい場合、一時停止ボタンをクリックして“レベル変更”を選択しないといけないので、少し手間。

　何故か筆者の環境だと一時停止のショートカットキーであるEscキーを押しても反応しない。他のアプリやゲーム、そしてタイトル画面だと使用できるので壊れてはいないはず。
　恐らく感覚的にEscキーを押してもメニューが開けないから、手間に感じるのだと思う。



[h1]●お薦めな点・感想等[/h1]

　バッジ作成時の割引券が手に入ったのと、好みのパズルゲームだったので購入した。

　基本的に指定数以内を目指してプレイしたが、五つぐらいのステージが指定数内クリアが出来なかった。
　と言うのも、後半になると30手前後が必要なステージも多いのでかなり長考して頭が痛くなってきて断念したのだ。それぐらいには歯ごたえのあるゲームだ。

　通常のクリアを目指す場合でも、ある程度の思考力が必要なので、全体的に難しめである。だから頭を使いたい時にはお薦めできる内容だと思う。

　指定された数がゲーム内だと完璧と書いてあるが、とあるステージでそれ以下の手でクリアできたので、開発者の想定を超えたようで嬉しかった。

[h1]Overall = 8/10[/h1]

My counselor had just passed away, Covid was effecting the world at an obscene rate, and my friends were all far away from me. Even worse, my anti-depressants were just not working. I really love the whole Quell series and Reflect might be my favorite one of them all. It offers the same sort of puzzles as the first one and adds in just enough new mechanics to keep things interesting, but not so many that things would turn overly gimmicky. Just playing through the game and collecting hidden gems is very relaxing and fun, but once again there is also the option of trying to complete every level in perfect moves - and that can get really dang difficult from time to time! Whether that's just a nice challenge or a frustrating feature depends on the player, but fortunately the game also has a really good hint system in case you end up needing some help. All in all this is one of my favorite puzzle games that you can easily just pick up and play no matter where you were when you last saved the game!

C'est un petit jeu de réflexion, idéal pour se relaxer après une journée de boulot.

The second instalment in the Quell series, Quell Reflect, builds upon the first game's framework and enhances the gameplay with new puzzle mechanics. Its look and feel isn't quite as melancholic but still nostalgic and relaxing in the same way. Aside from the steeper difficulty curve in comparison to its predecessor, everything else is in the same vein.

A few new mechanics, most notably the ability to control multiple drops in one level and the introduction of momentum-based moves, shake up the familiar puzzle gameplay. However, a handful of levels with up to 42 maximum moves to perfect are strewn into later sections in the game and can be tough nuts to crack. There's an ingame credit system that may be used to view the solution but working it out yourself without brute forcing it takes a considerable amount of time and dedication.

The underlying narrative is equally elusive as in Quell with only subsequent year dates and background images revealing a glimmer of a story. With a few new tracks added to the soundtrack, the music is once again soothing and a perfect match for a puzzle game such as this one.

It's overall a solid follow-up to Quell.

[h1]Quell Your Puzzle Addiction?  [i](A Quell Series review)[/i][/h1]

Slide, slide.. slide away many enjoyable hours being challenged by some deceptively well designed, compact puzzles in the [b]Quell Series[/b]. Your goal is to collect all the Pearls in the minimum number of moves & as a bonus, locate the hidden jewel found on each level. Simple right? Well the "Quells" can be deceiving .. as you will quickly find out.

Including the original [b]Quell[/b] & the sequels, [b]Quell Reflect[/b] & [b]Quell Memento[/b], each instalment are essentially clones the previous, introducing more & more varied puzzle elements to the rule set, increasing the complexity. Personally, I found the puzzle difficulty to vary considerably, with some perfect puzzle runs only taking a couple tries where others had me truly stumped for ages just trying to complete [i](let alone perfect)[/i]!

On average, progression was fairly steady throughout though. The best puzzles for me where those around 10-20ish moves, many still complex & challenging, but once the moves get 20+ it begins to get hard to keep track of the long sequences.

What I really liked in much of the puzzle design is the way you can break down the problem & make deductions from the layout presented to you. You may get a clue to which order you need to collect the Pearls based on their location/access or see obstacles you need to move or destroy in order, or what square you need to get your delicate raindrop to, or what to collect last.

Each little clue helps you formulate your strategy & is very satisfying to pull it all together to hear the chime of the perfect run. There is some great use of misdirection in level design & element placement, which keeps you guessing. The beauty & subtly in the designs is not immediately visible till you find the right path.

All instalments offer what must be close to 100 puzzles each. Each set of 4 puzzles makes up a window panel, with 3 window panels making up a year/tier [i](12 puzzles in total for each year, increasing to 16+ in Memento)[/i]. You can only progress to the next puzzle once you have completed the current one. This can be a bit frustrating if you get stuck for an extended period. I would have liked to see the set of 4 puzzles in a window panel unlocked together so you could mix it up a bit, perhaps with a percentage requirement to open up subsequent sets or years in advance.

Still the games are, generally speaking, forgiving offering instant undo/back & retry at the touch of a button, encouraging experimentation, plus solutions can be purchase with in-game Qoins if you really get stuck. Although I tried to avoid using the Qoins, there were some levels that bested me towards the end of the two sequels.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1384794903 The original [b]Quell[/b], I found to be the easiest since it offered the more basic puzzle mechanics & in-turn also had a nice, steadily increasing difficulty curve. That all changed when I hit [b]Quell Reflect[/b]. With the introduction of multiple raindrops, golden block gateways, transporter rings & poison raindrops. The challenge really ramped up & found myself using a few Qoins!

[b]Quell Memento[/b] continued to build on both of the previous instalments, with some creative new puzzle elements, such as lasers/light beams, illuminated squares, wormholes, roses that toggle spikes, power switches & ice cube blocks. These make the puzzles refreshing, different, greatly changing how you tackle each challenge. The downside to this is that now with so much element variety, many levels do become overly/unnecessarily complex lots of possible permutations. 

Also refreshed is the UI & introduction of some voice overs telling a story [i](hinted at in the first 2 games)[/i]. Some levels also offer a new timekeeper sub-level stages, each hidden inside a main level. These are particularly sinister ones, generally offering a hardcore challenge if you can find them.

Once I started playing I couldn't put the [b]Quell Series[/b] down for long, playing through all three instalments over the course of a few of weeks. The controls are responsive, & the instalments are well presented graphically with nice sound effects & serene music. There is a solid amount of content & the puzzles are engaging, varied & well designed.

My brain recieved a good workout! Highly recommended!

I'm going to review Quell, Quell Reflect, and Quell Memento all in one because there's a lot of comparing I'm going to do.

Essentially Quell and Quell Reflect are the same.  The layout, menu, feel, goals are all the same.  If you have one and loved it then get the other.  The puzzles themselves are different so it's just more of the same.  Quell Memento feels very different and has a slightly higher degree of difficulty I feel.  The feel of it is different as it now has a storyline, the stages are set up differently, and has different game components than the other two.

For Quell and Quell Reflect you are simply moving your ball(s) around with the arrows to collect all the pearls on the puzzle without dying from different types of traps.  Quell Momento changes this by having some that are collecting pearls and others where you're changing colors of tiles.  It's the same movements, but has more nuances to it.  Quell Reflect adds multiple balls while Quell only had one so extra mechanic, but not really that much more difficult.  Quell Memento might be better if you want a slightly higher degree of difficulty.

For each puzzle you will be solving it in the fewest moves trying to get the perfect.  You can complete it with more moves, it won't stop you if you go over.  So in that sense it can be a very relaxing puzzle.  It has a perfect set of moves and occasionally you can complete the puzzle in less moves.  This does not happen a lot. It's only required to find them in Quell Memento for the achievements. 

Each puzzle board has a second puzzle built in it where you find the hidden gem.  There are times when you see it and just have to navigate to it.  So for each board you're doing it over twice.  With Quell Memento, there are a bunch were you find a third hidden element which is a ring to take you to a secret board where you must solve that one twice for the moves and for a hidden object.

For Quell and Quell Reflect you will probably get all the achievements by just playing the game.  There are a few like getting caught in a loop or dying to a spike a certain amount of times that you might need to just replay a game a few times to collect, but maybe not.  I get those out of the way quickly as they are only like 5 or 15 times of something.  It's no big deal.  As long as you finish everything perfectly you will have all your achievements.  Not so for Quell Memento.  With Memento they added a bunch of other achievements, like forcing you to find a better than perfect board and completing it, changing a light bulb tile 200 times (that will NEVER happen through normal play), and others that you really need to go back and figure out how to do.  I got lucky and stumbled through a few by chance, but upon completing the game I still had 4 more to go.  I found the 200 times one really annoying to do.  There's an achievement that forces you just to leave it go at the right screen to get an achievement.  I don't really care for achievements like that.  I prefer how they did Quell and Quell Relect much better.

Overall, I liked the games.  I bought them in the Quell Collection and had fun with it.  I don't see myself replaying it though.  So if you're looking for that, I don't see it.  I didn't really care for Quell Memento that much.  I played it between Quell and Reflect and you could tell it was a later version, but I wasn't really thrilled with the changes to it.  I didn't care for doing a board three times and then doing the secret hidden board twice.  It became too much and I didn't know why not just add those boards as regular puzzles.  Doing a puzzle twice was okay.  By the third time I was really bored sick of it.  And if you screwed up on the secret board in a way that brought you back to the first, you had to redo the first to open up the entrance to the secret board again.  So there was just way too much repetition there.  I didn't like the achievements as I already stated, and I found the story and cleaning off the tile to get to the stages menu just extra work I didn't want to have to do.  I don't have complaints on Quell and Quell Reflect other than if you wanted a major step up in difficulty and a complete change in one from the other you're not going to get it.  But I like them both equally and really enjoyed doing them.  If you get stuck there are guides and videos to help you out.
